blocks.x: Utah's Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy approved a slate of new health AI pilots on Friday, among them one from Nolla Health, whose dermatology app assesses acne from patients' photographs. That pilot will test whether the app can prescribe initial medications and refills from a short list of topical drugs to adults in Utah with mild to moderate acne.

Human review is not removed up front. At first two physicians will review every prescription before it is sent, and only in later stages would they review prescriptions after the fact. All three companies need written approval from regulators before moving into those later phases, and none of the pilots have launched yet.

The other two approvals went to August AI, whose system will renew prescriptions for people with chronic conditions, and Expect Fitness, which will offer virtual pelvic floor therapy for women in the state.

The sandbox, formally the Artificial Intelligence Learning Laboratory, was created by state law in 2024. An earlier Utah pilot already lets an AI system renew medications without clinician oversight; the state medical licensing board asked for it to be suspended and regulators refused. A law and health policy professor at Stanford University has argued in a commentary that the contract behind that pilot is unclear about who is responsible if AI prescribing errors injure patients.
AIRS Medical has received Food and Drug Administration 510(k) clearance for SwiftSight Body Composition, its AI based MRI software for quantifying muscle and fat.

The software measures visceral and subcutaneous fat, abdominal and thigh muscle including muscle quality and bilateral balance, and liver fat using proton density fat fraction. It benchmarks those measurements against age and sex matched reference populations and puts them into a report with percentile rankings and visual summaries, the company said.
The firm is aiming the software at whole body and preventive imaging, weight management and wellness programs, and at repeat assessments over time. SimonMed Imaging will be its first customer.

NEJM AI has published an independent external validation of an AI system that reads dual stain cytology for triage in cervical cancer screening based on HPV testing. The full text is behind a subscription, so what follows comes from the published abstract and the study design figure.

blocks.cap: The study design: training cohorts, blinded external evaluation, algorithm lock in December 2024, then the independent validation cohort.

blocks.x: Screening based on HPV testing made molecular detection scalable, but deciding which screen positive people need further work up still depends on reading dual stain cytology by hand. That step is endorsed by guidelines yet limited by variation between readers and by the absence of standard automation.

The system, Cytoreader-Fusion, is an ensemble model that classifies whole slides and outputs calibrated probabilities. It was trained on 1,919 cases and evaluated under blinded honest broker oversight on 9,006 cases across four independent cohorts. Every preprocessing step, aggregation rule and decision parameter was fixed and locked before validation, and performance was measured against histologically confirmed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 or worse, not against agreement with human cytology readers.

In the fully independent cohort of 4,996 cases the locked system reached 88.3 percent sensitivity and 54.4 percent specificity for that end point, with no retraining or threshold tuning after the lock, and one classifier covered both slide preparation platforms. The authors present this as a high stringency validation framework for clinically deployable AI in population screening. It is a validation, not a trial, and not a deployment.
Communications Medicine has published an evaluation of how 20 open weight large language models respond to unsafe clinical instructions, the case where deference to authority would cause harm.

blocks.cap: The study pipeline: 501 synthetic variants and 100 real clinical cases, run under social pressure and mitigation conditions, with answers sorted into harmful and safe categories.

blocks.x: The team built 601 instances: 501 synthetic variants derived from 50 templates, plus 100 cases drawn from real de-identified intensive care records. Each instance was run under 21 framing conditions and four mitigation conditions, ten times each, producing 10,096,800 outputs. Each time the model picked one of four options, two potentially harmful actions and two safe ones, refusing or escalating.

Across all runs 1.18 million of 10.1 million outputs, or 11.7 percent, selected a potentially harmful option. A short reminder to verify or escalate unsafe requests cut that from 16.6 percent to 10.1 percent, a reduction of 6.5 percentage points, and the drop held in 19 of the 20 models. On the record derived cases the rate was far higher, falling from 46.6 percent to 24.5 percent.

Models were also inconsistent: in 80.4 percent of repeated ten run cells a model returned the same category of answer every time, with model level consistency ranging from 4.4 percent to 100 percent. The authors call the work a proof of concept that supplies an evaluation framework and state plainly that it does not estimate clinical risk in deployed systems. No patients were involved.

blocks.cap: Permission granted by Teladoc

blocks.x: Teladoc Health is adding new artificial intelligence capabilities to its virtual care platform for hospitals and health systems: a “contactless” approach to remotely monitoring patients’ vital signs and an AI scribe that records and transcribes clinical encounters to create notes. The scribing tool is now available; the vitals feature is in private preview and expected to be released broadly in December.

SoloVitals lets care teams track patients’ heart and respiratory rates without touching them: Solo devices with a camera capture patients' facial skin color and use an optical technique to measure changes in blood volume. SoloScribe is an ambient AI documentation feature for both in-person and virtual visits.

“Health systems are under intense pressure to do more, yet they are spending more time navigating a growing number of platforms, tools and vendors,” said Joby McKenzie, general manager of North American Health Systems at Teladoc Health.

After a net loss of $200.3 million in 2025, Teladoc lowered its 2026 revenue outlook in July to $2.36 billion to $2.45 billion, down 5% from earlier guidance, primarily due to its mental health division, BetterHelp.

This exploratory, multicenter, randomized, rater-blinded, multi-arm comparative trial aimed to evaluate the feasibility and exploratory clinical signals of an AI-facilitated telerehabilitation system across different intervention durations in early-stage Parkinson’s disease (PD).

One-hundred and twenty PD patients (Hoehn-Yahr stage ≤2.5) were randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio into short-term (1 month), medium-term (2 months), and long-term (3 months) training groups (15–30 min, 5 days/week). The primary outcome was the change in MDS-UPDRS Part III score from baseline to 3 months.

Final analysis included 71 participants. No significant differences were observed between groups for the primary motor outcome at 3 months. Post hoc responder analysis showed that the 3-month group had higher proportions reaching the exploratory cognitive responder threshold compared with the 1-month group. No falls or adverse events were recorded throughout the trial.

Because the primary endpoint was negative, attrition was high, no usual-care control was included, and the cognitive finding was limited to an exploratory post-hoc analysis, the authors say the findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating, requiring further validation in larger trials.
Clairity is broadening U.S. availability of its Clairity Breast AI-based breast cancer risk assessment platform through a partnership with consumer health testing company Everlywell.

Clairity Breast analyzes a single routine screening mammogram to predict a woman's five-year risk of developing breast cancer. The platform received De Novo authorization from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2025. It was previously available only at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Massachusetts and Invision Sally Jobe Imaging Center in Colorado.

Patients in the U.S. with a qualifying recent screening mammogram can now access the assessment through Everlywell's consumer platform, which includes physician order review, digital results delivery, and clinician-supported follow-up, Clairity said. The company was founded by breast imaging researcher Connie Lehman, MD, PhD.

Widespread AI adoption in a private radiology practice can produce measurable efficiency gains, according to a study published in JACR. European imaging experts assessed 10 AI tools from seven vendors over a nearly 5-year implementation across 20 outpatient imaging centers of the 3R Swiss Imaging Network.

“Infrastructure latency, not algorithm speed, was the primary barrier to clinical utility,” wrote lead author Dr. Sergey Morozov and colleagues. Cohorts included 97,000 exams for latency, 21,000 exams from 2025 for turnaround time, and a survey of 58 radiologists.

Active AI adoption reached about 91% of physicians. Median total latency was about 2.06 minutes, about 72% of it from data routing; AI results arrived after the report was finalized in about 7.2% of cases, from 3% for knee MRI to 13% for chest CT.

AI availability was associated with lower median turnaround times for trauma radiography (-26%) and knee MRI (-18%), while brain volumetry MRI showed no significant change. The program generated 0.69 FTE of capacity through trauma radiography alone.

blocks.cap: A radiologist reading mammograms at a reporting workstation. Source: Lunit.

blocks.x: A European health system has announced that it will replace radiologist second reads in breast screening with artificial intelligence. The rollout spans three hospitals in Sweden's Stockholm Region and covers between 200,000 and 250,000 breast imaging exams a year, with the AI acting as an independent second reader at regional scale.

Like most of Europe, and unlike the United States, Sweden has two radiologists independently review each mammogram as a quality check. The AI stands in for the second of those two readers, so one radiologist still reads every exam.

The groundwork was a prospective, population based study at Saint Goran hospital in Stockholm, which evaluated the system in the real world screening of more than 55,000 women. First year results presented at the RSNA meeting in 2024 showed a 15% increase in cancer detection and more than a 36% reduction in radiologist reading times.

That hospital has used the system since 2023, supporting around 200,000 breast exams over three years, and this is the vendor's second region wide rollout in Sweden after Dalarna County. The news follows a Berlin based company's announcement that it received the world's first approval for a breast triage tool that bypasses radiologist review entirely for normal mammograms.

Suki launched Ask, a tool that lets clinicians ask complex clinical questions using Wolters Kluwer’s UpToDate Expert AI API directly within the Suki for Clinicians app. Answers are grounded in UpToDate’s proprietary content, developed by more than 7,600 physician authors, editors and peer reviewers; it is the first product integration of the API.

Responses include transparent sourcing, medication and dosing considerations and links to supporting content. “Clinicians selected patient-specific insights 83% of the time across various queries, including diagnoses, dosages and safety considerations,” said Suki chief product officer Abhi Pathak.
Ask is available across Epic, Oracle Health, athenahealth and Meditech EHR systems. In late August, Suki also rolled out Suki Dictation, built natively inside Epic and Meditech EHRs.

The Ministry of Health and Welfare and the Korean Neuropsychiatric Association released the “Guidelines for Using Generative AI for Mental Health Purposes” on the 8th, ahead of Mental Health Day on the 10th. Their message: do not accept AI answers as medical judgment, and seek help from professionals in a mental health crisis.

The guidelines for all users contain 3 key messages and 21 recommendations. They advise checking a service's purpose, evidence base and personal data handling before use, and recommend: “Don't take what AI says about your condition as a conclusion” and “Keep your distance from AI, and talk to a person.” Children and adolescents, and guardians, were each given 7 recommendations.

In a Korea Institute for Health and Social Affairs survey (1,019 people), 68.8% of respondents had used generative AI for emotional purposes, and 14.6% had accepted AI's judgment as a medical diagnosis or used it to diagnose themselves with a mental illness. Among adolescents aged 15 to 18, 51.7% said they consider themselves somewhat dependent on AI.

Choi Jun-ho, chairman of the Korean Neuropsychiatric Association, stressed: “Since AI cannot replace professional assessment and treatment, it is important to get timely help from medical staff when needed.”

Epilepsy and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures often present with similar seizure-like manifestations but require fundamentally different management strategies. Misdiagnosis is common and can lead to prolonged diagnostic delays, unnecessary treatments, and substantial patient morbidity. Although prolonged video-electroencephalography is the diagnostic gold standard, its high cost and limited accessibility hinder timely diagnosis.

Here, we developed a low-cost, effective approach, EpiScreen, for early epilepsy detection by utilizing routinely collected clinical notes from electronic health records. Through fine-tuning large language models on labeled notes, EpiScreen achieved an AUC of up to 0.875 on the MIMIC-IV dataset and 0.980 on a private cohort of the University of Minnesota. In a clinician-AI collaboration setting, EpiScreen-assisted neurologists outperformed unaided experts by up to 14.3%.

Overall, this study demonstrates that EpiScreen supports early epilepsy detection, facilitating timely and cost-effective screening that may reduce diagnostic delays and avoid unnecessary interventions, particularly in resource-limited regions.

Real-time medication-safety auditing requires current laboratory and medication histories, yet EHRs may contain stale or missing decisive evidence. The authors present ClinicalGPT, an audit-ready foundation model using Clinical Trajectory Language to encode time, units, provenance, and observability.

Across seven health systems, they retrospectively evaluated 847,000 eligible high-risk medication orders. ClinicalGPT with hard constraints achieved 3.2 misses per 1000 orders, versus 9.4 for rules only, 6.1 for the original generic LLM comparator, and 4.8 for the strongest LLM comparator (RAG + LLM + rules). Its false-alert rate was 33.9, versus 38.7 for rules only.

The offline metric did not measure clinical actions, adverse drug events, or patient harm; the findings support comparative order-time auditing performance but do not establish clinical effectiveness or reduced patient harm.

blocks.cap: Photo: Lerner Children’s Pavilion at Hospital for Special Surgery

blocks.x: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has cleared AI software designed to improve pediatric bone age assessments. The 510(k) clearance covers Visiana’s BoneXpert, a machine learning software that determines bone age in patients ages 2 to 21 using the Greulich-Pyle method, intended to support pediatric radiologists in evaluating children with growth and pubertal disorders.

Manual assessment is a known challenge and can vary between readers. BoneXpert analyzes radiographs of either hand and provides an annotated image showing the bones it evaluated and their individual bone ages. It withholds a result when an image falls outside its validated scope; the radiologist remains responsible for the final assessment.

In a multicenter study at five U.S. sites, its root mean square error was 0.55 years, compared with 0.76 years for radiologists, with fewer results off by at least 1.5 years (1.7% vs. 6.4%). The software runs on-premise, so radiographs do not leave the institution.
BoneXpert has been used clinically in Europe since 2009 and is supported by more than 50 peer-reviewed studies. Visiana plans to release it in the U.S. in early October.

blocks.cap: prostate cancer PSA

blocks.x: An AI solution from RadNet subsidiary DeepHealth can help nearly 1 in 5 patients avoid prostate biopsies, according to new research in European Radiology comparing an AI risk-classification tool against radiologist-assigned PI-RADS scores on prostate MRI.

AI-assisted biopsy triage avoided nearly 19% of biopsies while maintaining 98.4% sensitivity for clinically significant cancer. The retrospective study covered nearly 800 subjects scanned between 2014 and 2025 in the U.S., Germany and the Netherlands, on equipment from five vendors.

The tool uses a simplified three-tier risk scale (low, medium, high) versus PI-RADS' five categories. It achieved non-inferior patient-level sensitivity and higher discrimination than PI-RADS, but lower lesion-level sensitivity, so researchers see it complementing PI-RADS, especially for equivocal PI-RADS 3 lesions, while radiologists retain responsibility for lesion mapping.

“These findings show how AI applications within our Prostate MR Solution can support clinicians at one of the most consequential decision points in prostate care,” said DeepHealth's Niccolò Stefani, MD.

blocks.cap: Across the UT System, the pilot grew 73% in recording clinicians and 80% in monthly notes over the last 12 months. (Pakorn Supajitsoontorn/GettyImages)

blocks.x: Abridge is expanding its clinical AI platform across the University of Texas System through an enterprise-wide agreement with UT REAL Health AI, giving the system's eight health institutions access while upholding local decision-making.

The deal builds on a pilot launched in 2025 with clinicians at five locations across outpatient, inpatient and emergency settings and more than 50 specialties. UT Health hospitals and clinics provided nearly 11.7 million outpatient visits in the last year.

“We are focused not only on expanding clinician access to ambient AI to strip away the mental clutter of clerical overhead, but equally on returning that focused, human presence back to patients at the bedside,” said UT REAL Health AI chair Peter McCaffrey, M.D.

Abridge says it works with 300 of the largest U.S. health systems and will support more than 100 million patient-clinician conversations this year. Last month it won an enterprise ambient AI contract with the VA.

Coreline Soft said on the 6th that its lung nodule diagnostic support software, AVIEW Lung Nodule CAD, has been listed as an officially certified AI software product by the Japan Radiological Society (JRS). Following approval last month from Japan's Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA), the company has secured a basis for linking the product to imaging diagnosis add-on fees.

With this certification, medical institutions that meet the facility standards for imaging diagnosis management add-on 3·4 can claim the add-on fee when they use the product. Certification of the product alone, however, does not apply to every hospital. Japan currently has 45 JRS-certified AI imaging diagnostic support software products, and the PMDA approval is the first for a Korean-developed CT-based lung nodule CAD.

After acquiring VUNO's Japanese chest CT AI assets last year, the company grew its customer hospitals to about 80 within 1 year, and also signed a supply contract with M3 AI for its cardiovascular software AVIEW CAC.

CEO Kim Jin-kook said, “By securing certification that meets hospitals' fee requirements following PMDA approval, the incentive for Japanese medical institutions to adopt AI and keep using it has become much clearer.”

Researchers ran a systematic quantitative analysis of ten GPT-5-based configurations on 161 clinician-validated real-world multimodal cases, scoring diagnostic accuracy, reasoning quality, retrieval accuracy, evidence integration and robustness to low-quality inputs.

They found important limitations, including image misinterpretation, inconsistent web search that sometimes degraded performance, and limited transparency in agentic workflows. Strengths included effective use of patient history, clear stepwise reasoning, plausible differentials, improved specificity with explicit reasoning, and relevant evidence retrieval.

The authors conclude that reliable real-world multimodal diagnosis depends more on transparent reasoning and high-quality inputs than on aggressive retrieval or complex agentic workflows, and that gaps in evidence integration and visual reasoning remain major barriers to routine clinical use.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has cleared an AI-powered platform, MRI2CT Inc.'s NextMR, that creates 3D bone visualizations from standard spine MRIs. The Israel-based vendor says its goal is to enable “MRI-only workflows in spine care,” producing detailed models of bone morphology without exposing patients to additional radiation from CT.
“Patients commonly begin their spine journey with an MRI, while detailed 3D visualization of bone may require another imaging step,” CEO Shmulik Shpiro said. “NextMR changes that paradigm.”

NextMR works with routine MRI sequences on 1.5T and 3T scanners and automatically generates its 3D bone output in under 60 seconds, viewable through a web interface. It was validated on an independent, retrospective dataset of 145 adults with paired MRI and CT images from sites in the U.S. and Israel.

blocks.cap: The FDA's second-tier priorities include finalizing guidance on pulse oximeters.

blocks.x: The Food and Drug Administration published its fiscal 2027 guidance priorities Thursday, setting itself the goal of finalizing and drafting artificial intelligence documents. Over the coming 12 months, the FDA's top priorities include finalizing guidance on marketing submissions and lifecycle management for AI-enabled devices and drafting generative AI advice.

The agency is also prioritizing the swift finalization of its guidance on premarket submissions of robotically assisted surgical devices, which it published in draft form last week. The FDA is accepting feedback on its priorities until Nov. 30.

The FDA published the draft AI-enabled device lifecycle guidance in January 2025. This year, it is prioritizing drafting evidentiary recommendations on generative AI-enabled conversational devices for mental disorders, a topic absent from last year's list but aligned with an August call for feedback on regulating generative AI.

Other priorities include air-purifying respirators, menstrual product testing and labeling, quality management systems, and a holdover on predetermined change control plans. Second-tier priorities include finalizing guidance on pulse oximeters.

Treatment-related adverse event documentation is labor-intensive and subject to inter-observer variability. VOICE-AE is a multi-stage pipeline integrating automatic speech recognition, speaker diarization and large language models for automated extraction and grading of CTCAE toxicities from clinician-patient audio recordings.

Encounters of prostate cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy were recorded; six blinded human raters graded 10 genitourinary/gastrointestinal toxicities from the same transcripts. 31 patients (39 encounters) yielded 390 encounter–toxicity assessments, 300 (76.9%) with a reference grade of 0.

VOICE-AE achieved a mean weighted kappa of 0.717. Exact CTCAE grade match was 82.6% and within-one-grade accuracy 99.2%, though a trivial always-grade-0 classifier would reach 76.9% and 93.6%. Performance was weaker at grades 1 and 2 (F1 0.58 and 0.57); binary detection sensitivity was 77.8%, specificity 89.0%.

VOICE-AE performed within the range of inter-expert agreement, supporting the feasibility of automated post-encounter AE documentation. Accuracy at grade ≥2 and detection of severe toxicity remain unproven.

blocks.cap: Professor Park Yu-kyung, Department of Pediatrics, Asan Medical Center.

blocks.x: Professor Park Yu-kyung of the Department of Pediatrics at Asan Medical Center presented the hospital's experience running a pediatric RRS and its use of DeepCARS, an AI-based medical device for managing cardiac arrest risk, at VUNO's global pediatric patient safety symposium on September 19. In clinical practice, there have been cases where it flagged high-risk patients earlier than existing scoring systems, leading to intervention by the medical team.

Asan Medical Center introduced a pediatric rapid response team (PMET) in 2012, then added the APPLE score in 2020 and PMAS in 2022, followed by DeepCARS last year. Children whose DeepCARS score exceeds 90 or rises by 30 points or more over a short period are flagged for screening by a pop-up alarm. Park said, "We are finding it useful."

A girl aged 3 years and 11 months, admitted for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, was caught by the rapid response team after her DeepCARS score rose to 95 following ATG administration. Because some information, such as respiratory rate, had not been entered, the DeepCARS score rose before the APPLE score; the patient improved after transfer to the PICU and treatment.

blocks.cap: Asan Medical Center uses DeepCARS in its pediatric rapid response system. Photo: presentation materials by Professor Park Yu-kyung

blocks.x: There are limitations. Because monitoring is not real-time and continuous, vital signs that went unrecorded were hard to capture for both the APPLE score and DeepCARS, and false alarms are frequent during tests. Park added that AI should move toward also explaining why a score came out high and with what level of confidence it was assessed.

History-taking is central yet constrained by limited clinical resources. The researchers designed a pre-consultation LLM agent for history-taking using a dual-agent architecture with skills-engineered symptom-oriented logic trees, and ran a randomized clinical trial at a tertiary ophthalmic hospital in Guangzhou, China.

Between May 10 and June 10, 2025, 172 of 175 approached patients with non-emergency appointments were randomized 1:1 to the LLM agent or ophthalmology residents. The agent achieved better pre-consultation quality by MedHistory score (adjusted mean difference 17.7 points; 95% CI 14.1 to 21.3), higher patience and empathy ratings, and longer interactions (median 11.2 vs 3.1 minutes).

Test recommendation performance did not differ significantly. Exploratory analyses showed superior diagnostic accuracy from history alone (F1 0.85 vs 0.68), while ocular signs improved residents more, narrowing the gap. The authors suggest a hybrid workflow where clinicians focus on physical examination and diagnostic synthesis.

blocks.cap: Study in The Lancet suggests AI could improve patient-physician relationships.

blocks.x: Can AI safely assess patients’ needs before they step into a doctor’s office? A study led by researchers at Google and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) and published in The Lancet today, offers an encouraging first look. As Google’s first-ever publication in the main journal of The Lancet, this research marks a significant milestone.

In a real-world clinical study at BIDMC’s ambulatory primary care clinic, 98 patients consulted AMIE, our research diagnostic AI chatbot, ahead of urgent care visits. Supervising physicians monitored the interactions in real time, and not a single conversation needed to be interrupted based on predefined safety criteria. And clinicians reported that the AI summaries helped them prepare for visits in 75% of cases and influenced their approach to care in more than half. AMIE’s differential diagnoses also matched the doctors’ final diagnoses 90% of the time.

While larger clinical trials are needed to assess patient-facing AI at scale, the findings suggest the potential for AI to enhance the patient-physician relationship and ease the strain on healthcare workers. And they demonstrate meaningful progress as we push the boundaries of what’s possible for AI in science and health.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma comprises classical and basal-like molecular subtypes that differ in prognosis and treatment response, but transcriptomic subtyping is limited by cost, turnaround time and tissue requirements. The researchers asked whether these subtypes can be inferred directly from routine H&E-stained whole-slide images using deep learning.

They analyzed 689 patients with paired histology and RNA-sequencing data from the Pancreatic Cancer Action Network (n = 506) and The Cancer Genome Atlas (n = 183). Their model, PanSubNet, integrates cellular morphology with tissue architecture to predict subtype.

PanSubNet distinguished high-confidence classical and basal-like tumors with a mean AUC of 90.3% in internal validation and 84.0% in independent external validation. In metastatic disease, its predicted subtypes significantly stratified overall survival and flagged aggressive tumors among transcriptionally discordant cases.
The authors say the approach offers a rapid, tissue-sparing complement to transcriptomic profiling where molecular testing is limited or impractical.

A new analysis of the FDA’s AI-enabled medical device database, published in Academic Radiology, details how the technology’s regulatory standing has evolved. Stella K. Kang, MD, of Columbia University Irving Medical Center and colleagues characterized 1,094 radiology AI devices authorized through December 2025.

Annual authorizations increased by 42% during the timeframe studied, though the functional makeup stayed relatively stable: image management and processing systems made up 38% of devices, imaging systems 33% and interpretive AI tools 23%. Multi-finding devices rose from 4% to 18%.

Median FDA review time was shorter for OEM devices than non-OEM ones, 118 versus 138 days. Predetermined change control plan authorization rose from just under 1% in 2020–2023 to nearly 9% in 2025, a sign that some software modifications can be managed within an existing regulatory framework.

The Department of Health and Human Services announced a set of new initiatives aimed at speeding up clinical trials by incorporating more artificial intelligence and computational models and moving away from sharply delineated trial phases, as U.S. officials work to compete with China and other countries.

The centerpiece five-year program, dubbed SURPASS — “Simulation-augmented, Real-time Platform Adaptive Seamless Trials” — will kick off later this fall by accepting “ground-breaking ideas from cross-disciplinary teams in statistics, AI, and clinical trial design, operations, and regulation.”

HHS is launching the program through the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health. The initial announcement did not note how much funding was designated, nor whether participants would be offered more flexibility or resources.

Former FDA commissioner Scott Gottlieb argues clinical AI is following the path laboratory developed tests took: academic medical centers such as Duke Health, Johns Hopkins and NYU Langone build and deploy their own models largely outside FDA device oversight. That encourages experimentation but can keep useful tools from spreading and creates a two-tier market that disadvantages commercial developers.
He cites a national survey finding 65% of US hospitals use AI models, while only 44% of those using predictive models evaluated them for bias.

Gottlieb proposes that Congress create a CLIA-like certification route: the FDA would certify health systems, which would be responsible for validation, subgroup performance checks, change control, drift monitoring and regular reporting, with requirements scaled to risk. Lower-risk tools would need analytical validity first; higher-risk tools would need premarket clinical evaluation. Fully autonomous systems, patient-facing diagnostics and models offered outside the institution would stay under conventional device regulation.

Conversational AI chatbots are increasingly linked to emerging or worsening psychotic symptoms, a phenomenon the authors call "AI psychosis." Prior evidence was mostly case reports, viewpoints and simulations.

Researchers at Vanderbilt University Medical Center retrospectively reviewed behavioral health progress notes from December 1, 2022, to April 15, 2026, for patients with AI-related keywords and a documented psychotic-disorder diagnosis. Two raters classified AI interactions as neutral, AI psychosis (chatbot use that worsened psychosis) or AI-related psychotic content, and sorted AI psychosis cases into four types: catalyst, amplifier, coauthor and object.

Of 578,058 records (215,712 unique patients), 187 encounters from 73 patients met criteria. 28 patients (0.013% of those receiving mental health care) were in the AI psychosis group. ChatGPT was the documented product in 15 cases (53.6%), and 24 interactions (85.7%) were documented after the May 2024 release of GPT-4o. 60.7% of the AI psychosis group were in a first psychotic episode, vs 17.6% of the neutral group. Amplifier was the most common type (64.3%).

The authors note the rise after GPT-4o coincides with documented sycophancy in that model, but the design cannot establish causation. They conclude that routine assessment of AI use during psychiatric encounters appears warranted.

AI training and deployment in healthcare are challenging due to diverse data, a complex spectrum of tasks and important privacy needs. The authors introduce MedGemma, a collection of medical vision-language foundation models based on Gemma 3.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Overview of the MedGemma models.

blocks.x: MedGemma demonstrates advanced medical understanding and reasoning across images, text and multiple imaging domains, exceeding similarly sized generative models while keeping the general capabilities of the Gemma base models. On out-of-distribution tasks it improves on the base models by 2.6–10% in medical image question answering, 15.5–18.1% in chest X-ray finding classification and 10.8% in agentic evaluations.

Fine-tuning MedGemma can be more effective than fine-tuning base Gemma 3 for medical tasks, particularly with limited training data. The team also introduces MedSigLIP, a medically tuned vision encoder derived from SigLIP that powers MedGemma's visual understanding and matches or beats many specialized medical image encoders.

blocks.cap: Fig. 2: Examples of open-ended multimodal question answering with MedGemma 4B.

blocks.x: Any government that sells patient data is “betraying the trust” of its people, a leading expert on AI in health has said.

Speaking at the European Health Forum Gastein earlier this month, Ricardo Baptista Leite, chief executive officer of HealthAI—a non-profit group focused on promoting the safe, responsible, and regulated use of AI in healthcare—urged governments not to buy or sell patient data and to condemn those that do.

Leite, a Portuguese-Canadian doctor, also warned of a knowledge and power imbalance between the “tech bros” running AI companies and civil society—an imbalance he said could lead to greater health inequalities.

His comments come as pressure mounts on NHS England to end its health data contract with Palantir. The US company has been handling the NHS’s federated data platform since it won the contract in 2023.

Euan Ashley, chair of the Department of Medicine at Stanford, sat down with Claude and asked it to analyze his entire genome, following the framework a 30-person team used in 2009 to interpret Stephen Quake's genome over nearly a year.

Despite a decade-old genome file, Claude re-identified many key findings, including two copies of the APOE ε4 variant linked to Alzheimer's risk, no major variant for a rare inherited disorder, and DPYD and CYP2C19 variants affecting drug response. It warned the file lacked enough data for reliable risk scores. The interaction used around 400,000 tokens and cost approximately $5; most of the half-hour was spent waiting for databases to load.

Ashley argues that as consumers upload genomes into systems such as Claude or ChatGPT, the field needs standards for what a medical-grade genomic interpretation should include: well-characterized reference genomes, a catalog of hard-to-sequence medically significant genes, and disclosures from labs and AI developers on what their systems detect reliably. “Today, however, what’s scarce may be reliability.”

blocks.cap: Getty Images

blocks.x: AI has quickly become integrated into Americans' lives, with 40% of respondents saying they use AI at least once daily, according to an Ipsos survey of 254 U.S. patients conducted in March for Wolters Kluwer. About 1 in 4 said they pursued healthcare sooner after using AI to research symptoms or conditions.

But only about 30% would use AI to find a provider, 28% to create a diet, workout or sleep plan and 19% to navigate insurance coverage. Trust issues drive the reluctance: over 70% worry about the privacy of their protected health information, and patients are also concerned about AI bias (72%) and hallucinations (69%).

A vast majority said a human expert should validate AI-generated health responses, and nearly half said AI tools used for health advice should undergo federal testing and approval, similar to new medications.

Adolescents and young adults (AYAs) with hereditary cancer predisposition face high lifetime cancer risk, yet no models existed to support their understanding of that risk. This randomized clinical trial tested an electronic chatbot-based cancer risk communication tool, AYA Risk Information and Screening Education, at Dana-Farber, Emory/Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta, the University of Chicago and Utah’s Huntsman Cancer Institute between December 2022 and May 2025.

Participants were English speakers aged 12 to 24 with 1 of 9 hereditary cancer predisposition syndromes. The chatbot gave syndrome-specific risk and screening information, with resource pages to learn, plan screening, share with peers, connect to support groups and grow through coping support.

Of 798 AYAs assessed, 106 were randomized (54 chatbot, 52 control). After the clinic visit, 78% of the chatbot group versus 37% of controls had accurate knowledge of their cancer risk by age 30 (OR, 3.50; P = .005). Gains in screening knowledge and reductions in distress were not statistically significant.
The authors conclude that pairing a clinic visit with personalized, accurate electronic information improved risk knowledge without increasing distress.

AI may be on par with radiologists for finding prostate cancer on MRI, according to research published October 13 in Radiology. A team led by Anindo Saha, PhD, from Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, found an AI system achieved diagnostic performance comparable to radiologists for Gleason grade group ≥2 prostate cancer across external diagnostic and screening datasets.

blocks.cap: Prostate MRI exams illustrating AI detection of Gleason grade group ≥2 cancers across international sites. RSNA

blocks.x: The SCARLET-1 study included 22,445 prostate MRI exams from 21,252 men across 46 cities in 22 countries. The AI reached external AUCs of 0.86 in the diagnostic setting and 0.89 and 0.84 in two screening settings, with 83.0% to 87.9% agreement with radiology readings.

Performance varied across 25 sites and with image quality. "These findings support a potential role for AI in extending prostate MRI interpretation, particularly where subspecialty expertise is limited," the team wrote, adding that safe clinical use will require local testing and longitudinal performance monitoring.

One-third of the world's 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures uncontrolled by medication. Implantable devices can detect impending seizures, missed medication and impaired cognition, but cannot share this information with patients in real time.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Platform overview.

blocks.x: The researchers present an inpatient prototype that links scalp and intracranial EEG to a secure, large language model-based AI that communicates bidirectionally through a smartphone app. It notifies patients of clinical events and trends, records symptoms and responses, and uses their feedback to retrain its seizure detector.

The platform was validated in 13 patients undergoing video-EEG monitoring. Patients responded to 67.2% of real-time seizure alerts. In a pseudoprospective simulation, fine-tuning with patient annotations alone reduced false alarms by 80.9%, without expert intervention.

It has emerged that 2672 clinical trial result documents on Uiyakpum Anjeon Nara, the drug safety portal run by the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS), could be downloaded from outside without separate authentication. Of these, 839 contained company information set to private, and 2208 contained the mobile phone numbers of staff in charge.

blocks.cap: Photo: National Assembly Television.

blocks.x: At the National Assembly audit of the MFDS on the 13th, People Power Party lawmaker Lee So-hee said her office downloaded the documents without any login or password, using the generative AI service ChatGPT. "We did not hack anything; we obtained the data through ChatGPT, which anyone can use," Lee said. The data included clinical trial results and safety evaluation information such as efficacy and adverse reactions.

Lee noted that over the past 10 years the MFDS had kept 95 of 96 related disclosure cases private. MFDS Minister Oh Yu-kyoung said the ministry learned of the exposure on the 12th and blocked access early on the 13th. "We are grateful for being alerted to the problem of information access using AI, and we are taking the matter seriously," Oh said.

Despite growing clinical adoption of artificial intelligence in radiology, fewer than one in five commercially available models are cleared for paediatric use. Existing systems are trained predominantly on adult data and generalize poorly to neonates, yet efficient strategies for repurposing them without data sharing or large-scale local data curation are lacking.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Summary of continual learning paradigm and benchmark comparisons.

blocks.x: Here we present an international retrospective study of neonatal chest radiographs from 30 neonatal intensive care units across 20 countries and territories, evaluating continual learning as a privacy-preserving approach to adapt a deep learning model for adult endotracheal tube assessment to neonatal care. Each hospital contributed 50 radiographs for sequential model retraining without centralized data pooling.

Continual learning achieved lower anatomical landmark localization error (0.67 cm versus 1.29 cm for hospital-specific fine-tuning and 4.30 cm for adult-only models) at 29 of 30 sites, with improved detection of deep intubations at 27 of 30 sites. These findings demonstrate that privacy-preserving collaborative learning can address critical gaps in paediatric AI deployment.

AI tools are increasingly used for health information seeking, but their performance in layperson respiratory diagnosis and triage remains uncertain. Researchers assessed LungDiag, a task-constrained WeChat-based GPT-4o chatbot with a respiratory knowledge layer, against conventional mobile web search in a prospective, multicentre, single-blind, randomized simulated-case comparison.

Between April and June 2025, 2,400 adults without formal medical training at 24 Chinese healthcare systems were randomly assigned 1:1 to LungDiag assistance or browser-based search, with AI search functions disabled in the control arm.

blocks.cap: Fig. 1: Study flowchart.

blocks.x: In the primary analysis of 2,176 questionnaires, LungDiag achieved higher overall accuracy than the control (70.0% versus 55.4%), a risk difference of 14.6 percentage points. The largest difference was for diagnosis items (81.2% versus 54.5%), whereas triage gains were smaller (53.4% versus 47.1%). LungDiag required a longer completion time (median 527 s versus 461 s).

blocks.cap: Fig. 2: Crude pooled item-level accuracy for the LungDiag group and the web search control group.

blocks.x: The authors note the findings do not establish effects on real-world care-seeking, diagnostic delay or clinical outcomes.

Artificial intelligence-enabled quantification and analyses of brown adipose tissue (BAT) activity uncover links between BAT and a healthier metabolic profile along with lower rates of psychiatric disease.

The team expanded its cohort of 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans taken for clinical purposes at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center to 101,243 patients, 8,897 of them BAT positive, and analysed associations across all diagnostic codes.

A machine learning approach (TriDFusion) semi-automatically measured total and depot-specific BAT metabolic activity in 8,709 patients. Higher BAT activity was associated with a stepwise reduction in type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease and congestive heart failure, even after controlling for age, BMI, sex and outside temperature.

BAT presence was also associated with a lower prevalence of anxiety and depression. Medication analyses linked angiotensin receptor blocker use to BAT presence, and proof-of-concept experiments confirmed that losartan activates brown adipocytes through a PPARγ-dependent mechanism — showing the approach can identify drugs that could be repurposed to activate BAT.

blocks.cap: The artificial intelligence analyses images of suspicious skin lesions in minutes

blocks.x: Staff at an NHS clinic using artificial intelligence (AI) to detect skin cancer sooner have said the technology could be a "game changer". The dermatology team at St Luke's Hospital in Bradford adopted the system in April; 32 patients can now be seen in each session, compared to 24 before.

The system, DERM (Deep Ensemble for the Recognition of Malignancy), is made by Skin Analytics, which claims it is 99.9% accurate at ruling out melanoma. A healthcare assistant takes three photographs of the lesion and the system analyses them in minutes; benign cases are discharged with advice and suspicious ones referred to a specialist.

blocks.cap: The hospital trust said artificial intelligence has helped staff see one-third more patients in clinics

blocks.x: Every image is double-checked by a clinician. Unnecessary biopsies have dropped by about 10%, according to the trust. Consultant plastic surgeon Zakir Shariff said it has had a "big impact" on waiting times.

blocks.cap: Plastic surgeon Zakir Shariff said the AI has had a big impact on waiting times

blocks.x: NICE has recommended the technology for NHS use for the next three years while evidence is collected. It is deployed in 40 NHS trusts, and Bradford was the first in Yorkshire to adopt it.

Researchers evaluated electronic health record developer compliance with federal transparency requirements for AI-enabled predictive decision support interventions. Developers are required to publicly report on risk analysis, mitigation, governance, and on eight other attributes.

Across 35 developers, reporting was inconsistent and often incomplete, with substantial variation in structure and detail, yet all developers were certified as meeting the requirements. Results suggest a need for standardized reporting and more rigorous certification review.

Influential lobbying groups for doctors and hospitals, a health insurer, technology companies, and representatives from state governments met behind closed doors in Washington, D.C., in early October to develop guidelines for how to regulate artificial intelligence in the practice of medicine.

Executives from the American Medical Association, American Hospital Association, AI company Anthropic, and insurer Elevance Health are part of a 22-member AI workgroup convened by the Federation of State Medical Boards (FSMB). Its recommendations would be open for feedback before being formally adopted.

The goal is to draft guidelines to aid local medical boards, with "particular attention … to AI tools that perform clinical functions with limited or no direct physician supervision," FSMB president and CEO Humayun Chaudhry told STAT. A draft could be made public in "weeks to months" and could ultimately form the basis of state legislation.
The AMA, medical boards, and a conservative think tank are all jostling to control how autonomous clinical AI is regulated. The rest of the story is for STAT+ subscribers.

The government has today, 6 October 2026, confirmed it will accept all 44 recommendations made by the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, published 10 September. Alongside the response, the MHRA is opening applications for the third phase of AI Airlock, its regulatory sandbox for AI-enabled medical devices.

A central conclusion of the Commission was that AI-enabled medical devices should be assessed and monitored throughout their working life, instead of over-relying on one-time assessments. AI Airlock Phase 3, backed by three years of additional government funding, will focus on post-market surveillance and lifecycle regulation.

The MHRA will issue draft guidance by December 2026 on managing changes to AI-enabled devices as they adapt over time, and will consult next year on how to qualify and classify them. Other commitments include staged authorisation pathways allowing promising AI tools to be used in the NHS earlier under close supervision. A full implementation roadmap will be published by Spring 2027.

Lawrence Tallon, the MHRA's Chief Executive, said the Commission, led by NHS doctors, "has given us a clear and ambitious blueprint". A webinar for applicants takes place on 22 October; the first wave of innovators will be selected in November 2026.
A cross-sectional study published Oct. 15 in JAMA analyzed clinicians with NPI-verified OpenEvidence accounts from Jan. 1, 2024, through June 30, 2026.

Over the 2.5-year period, 952,008 clinicians, including 556,200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries. Monthly active users grew from 355 to 703,265, and average monthly queries per active user rose from 18.0 to 39.5.

Nurse practitioners and physician assistants (44.5 queries per active user-month each) outpaced physicians (37.1). Use was highest in oncology and hematology, internal medicine and family medicine, and lowest in ophthalmology, radiology and orthopedics.

Most queries (51.9%) addressed clinical decision-making, chiefly treatment and management (33.1%); diagnosis accounted for 13.9%. Queries outside a physician's own specialty ranged from 35% among oncologists to 88% among emergency physicians.

blocks.cap: The AMA framework sets four questions for assessing clinical AI agents.

blocks.x: The American Medical Association released a governance framework for AI agents used to perform clinical tasks, built around four questions: what clinical function the AI performs, what demonstrates it can do so and what happens if it fails, what it should be permitted to do and under what conditions, and who is responsible for the risks and outcomes.

Because agentic tools can complete multi-step tasks without human oversight, an inaccurate or biased decision could cause significant patient harm before a clinician can intervene. “As AI capabilities advance, evidence, authority, oversight and accountability must remain aligned in service of better patient care,” the framework states.

In a recent survey of 250 U.S. healthcare leaders, about 28% said their organization has deployed agentic AI and 44% are piloting it. In the absence of substantive federal AI regulation, industry groups are providing guidance; 47 states introduced over 250 AI bills impacting healthcare in 2025.

Phenotyping is fundamental to rare disease diagnosis, but manually curating structured phenotypes from clinical notes is labor intensive and difficult to scale. Existing AI approaches optimize individual components but do not operationalize the full workflow.

The researchers developed RARE-PHENIX, an end-to-end AI framework that combines large language model-based phenotype extraction, ontology-grounded standardization to Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, and supervised ranking of HPO terms.

It was trained on data from 2,671 patients across 11 Undiagnosed Diseases Network sites and externally validated on 16,357 clinical notes from 143 patients at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Its prioritized HPO terms were highly concordant with clinician curation, and it may support human-in-the-loop phenotyping in real-world settings.

Emergency department crowding is associated with delayed treatment and increased mortality, and proactive staffing requires reliable short-term demand forecasts. Most operational models rely on temporal or weather patterns.

Researchers tested whether community-level social determinants of health (SDoH) improve hourly ED demand prediction compared with weather, using XGBoost on 213,138 encounters aggregated into 22,883 hourly observations at a tertiary teaching hospital in Wuhan, China.

Models with dynamic SDoH features consistently outperformed weather-only models. The composite model reached an RMSE of 3.48 and an MAE of 2.62 visits per hour (R² 0.68), errors of about 2 to 3 patients per hour, suggesting practical use for short-term staffing and capacity planning.

The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has set out plans to translate cutting-edge scientific and technological innovation into better health outcomes for patients across all four nations of the UK, in its 2030 Strategy.

By 2030 the MHRA aims to be more patient-centred, support faster access to safe, effective treatments, and have more data-connectivity and global influence. Health innovation minister James Frith said the strategy will help the MHRA keep pace with the latest innovations in AI, data and medicine.
Chief executive Lawrence Tallon said AI is transforming both regulated products and how organisations are run, and that such developments challenge traditional regulatory models.

On AI, the MHRA commits to develop an AI-enabled Clinical Trial Protocol Checker, publish an AI Medicines Development Action Plan in 2027, establish an MHRA Centre for AI and Digital Health, and create a modern, adaptive regulatory framework for AI as a medical device. It will also use AI to analyse real-world data and identify potential safety issues earlier.
Other pledges include cutting the scientific advice service from 90 to 45 days, halving the initial assessment target for qualifying Phase 1 trials to 14 days, and a Women's Health Plan.

Seers, a wearable AI diagnostic monitoring company, said on the 16th that it has received approval from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) under the Abu Dhabi Department of Health (DoH) for the national health screening project it is pursuing with SEHA Clinics, the UAE's largest public healthcare network, and has begun the project in earnest.

The project is the final pilot for introducing AI arrhythmia screening into the national health screening program, which the UAE government provides to its citizens aged 40 and over 1 time per year. The UAE's national health screening currently does not include arrhythmia screening tests. Seers was selected as the sole contractor for the project through a tender late last year.

Seers will run AI ECG screening based on mobiCARE™ for about 100 screening participants to verify clinical effectiveness and operational fit, with the goal of being applied exclusively in the national health screening program from next year. Once included, it could serve about 280,000 people aged 40 and over each year, and revenue attributable to Seers is expected to exceed $100 per test.

Seers has verified clinical effectiveness with 3,000 examinees at 5 medical institutions, including Seoul National University Hospital, and operates AI arrhythmia screening at KMI Korea Medical Institute and the Korea Association of Health Promotion's Medicheck, among others. The company's strategy is to start with the UAE and expand the business to GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council) countries.

Kim Sung-jong, vice president (CBO), said, "We will successfully carry out this project to enter the UAE national health screening program and, building on that, expand our AI cardiovascular screening business to GCC countries."

A radiology department is detailing how it uses natural language processing to help root out screening-eligible patients from the health system's electronic health record. Lung cancer screening uptake remains low at about 18% nationally, experts detail Oct. 12 in the Journal of the American College of Radiology.

One key barrier is incomplete or inaccurate structured smoking history in the EHR. To address this, the University of California, Irvine, developed an NLP tool that extracts smoking info and identifies screening-eligible patients from free-text clinical notes.

The retrospective study included nearly 28,000 patients aged 50 or older with almost 41,000 EHR notes from 2018 to 2023. A rule-based NLP pipeline was built from 50 manually reviewed notes and refined on a separate 2,000 notes. Against 2,000 human-annotated notes, NLP showed nearly 84% agreement on screening eligibility.

"NLP-derived smoking status and LCS eligibility demonstrated high concordance with manual review and identified more than three times as many screening-eligible patients as structured EHR data," corresponding author Gelareh Sadigh, MD, and colleagues concluded, calling NLP "a practical and scalable approach" that works "without changing physician workflow."

Multimodal research-grade MRI scans show potential for differentiating Parkinson's disease (PD) from multiple system atrophy (MSA), but clinical translation is limited by cost, acquisition time, and processing burden. The authors developed a T1-weighted structural MRI-based machine learning model to differentiate Parkinsonism and generalized it to routine anisotropic 2D clinical MRI.

blocks.cap: From multimodal benchmark to clinical signature, research-grade validation and the external clinical-MRI cohort.

blocks.x: Using a multicenter cohort of 969 participants and a hierarchical discovery–verification–translation framework, a multimodal benchmark model achieved an AUROC of 0.98, while the streamlined unimodal T1-Top20 model achieved 0.93 for multiclass discrimination (healthy controls, PD, MSA).

blocks.cap: ROC curves and the combined Top-20 feature set for final classification.

blocks.x: For PD vs MSA, the frozen T1-Top20 model achieved a pooled AUROC of 0.88 in the external research-grade cohort (n = 227) and identified 19 of 25 who phenoconverted from idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder to PD. The generalized model achieved a pooled AUROC of 0.84 in the clinical-MRI cohort (2D T1, n = 303).

blocks.cap: Photo: National Assembly Television

blocks.x: The Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service (HIRA) was rebuked at the National Assembly Health and Welfare Committee's parliamentary audit on the 16th after it emerged that it had deleted past medical imaging data, citing a lack of storage space, and had not properly put in place deletion criteria or data standardization.

Rep. Kwon Chil-seung of the Democratic Party pressed HIRA on the volume of medical images it holds, saying, "People call these days the AI era, but if you look at the substance, it is an era of fighting over data."

blocks.cap: Photo: National Assembly Television

blocks.x: According to the data, medical image holdings were about 5 million to 13 million per year from 2021 to 2024, but reached about 230 million in 2025 and about 200 million in just the first 9 months of this year. Kwon said, "That is because the medical images from before 2024 were deleted," estimating that about 90% of past data had in effect been deleted, and pointed out that there were no deletion criteria either.

The data standardization rate stayed at about 1 to 3%, and a data demonstration lab that cost 2 billion won over 3 years has recorded 0 uses by outside AI developers since 2021. At the end of the questioning, critics also said it was "as good as wiping out all of its assets."
HIRA President Hong Seung-kwon acknowledged the storage problem and the lack of internal management standards, saying, "We will standardize high-quality data that industry can use for AI training."

Researchers at Seoul National University Hospital tested whether humans and large language models can tell real chest x-rays from AI-generated ones, in a study published Oct. 13 in the Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine.

The set held 160 chest x-rays: 40 real and 120 synthetic images from three AI pipelines. Two radiologists, two general practitioners and three LLMs (Gemini 3.5 Flash, GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet) judged each one.

Gemini 3.5 Flash (77.9% balanced accuracy) and the thoracic radiologist (75.8%) did best, with no significant difference; the general practitioners performed near chance. Radiologists caught diffusion-model images more often (82%–100%) than LLMs (32%–72%), while LLMs were more specific on real images. Overall agreement was poor (Fleiss' kappa 0.213).

Neither humans nor LLMs appear suitable as the primary safeguard, the authors concluded. They recommend treating image provenance as data governance, using cryptographic content credentials or watermarking, with visual review as a secondary control.
Researchers developed an AI model, AI-OsRM, to predict osteoporosis and reduced bone mineral density (BMD) from chest radiographs, reports npj Digital Medicine.

AI-OsRM was developed using 46,478 paired chest X-ray and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) examinations from 26,757 patients collected at a tertiary referral hospital between 2016 and 2022, using a ResNet-based architecture with masked autoencoder pretraining.

External validation covered three cohorts: a temporally separated hospital cohort (SNUH; n = 6,391) and two health checkup cohorts (HPC, n = 24,132; YSMC, n = 122,535). AUROC was 0.88 in SNUH for both osteoporosis and reduced BMD, and 0.93 and 0.92 for osteoporosis in HPC and YSMC.

Simulations showed AI-OsRM prescreening could cut DXA use by about 50% while still detecting 98-99% of osteoporosis cases and 80-90% of reduced BMD cases, suggesting a prescreening tool to optimize DXA utilization.

General-purpose AI agents can now work through files and applications on a user's computer. Products such as ChatGPT Work, ChatGPT Codex, Claude Cowork, and Claude Code bring these abilities to consumer apps, write Mahmud Omar, Eyal Klang and Girish N Nadkarni in The Lancet Digital Health.

Such agents could run on a clinician's home computer or a hospital workstation. With computer use, an agent captures the screen at each step and sends it to the developer's servers, so it sees whatever is displayed and acts with the clinician's login. An agent booking a follow-up could capture an unrelated diagnosis in a neighbouring panel.
Permission to operate an application does not establish which information is appropriate for each task, the authors argue, and clinicians cannot be expected to review every screenshot.

They propose a standard institutional process, modelled on the tiered structure of IRBs, run as an alignment and agentic safety board. Approval would specify the task, accessible data, tools, recipients and retention; new capabilities would trigger review. The agent's access should remain proportional to the work delegated.

A cross-sectional study in JAMA Network Open surveyed 1,185 US adults (June 17 to July 26, 2024) on whether they prefer faster AI responses or slower, health-professional-reviewed responses to patient portal messages, and how they weigh AI options for mental health support.

For logistical messages such as scheduling and refills, 57.4% preferred a fast AI answer; for general messages, 50.6%. For medical messages, 63.1% preferred waiting for a health professional to review the response.
For mental health support, 63.9% most endorsed a human therapist available in 3 months, ahead of therapist-monitored AI in 1 month (50.2%) and AI alone available immediately (44.3%).

Results were stratified by birth generation and other factors. The authors conclude people are more open to faster AI for low-stakes tasks than for medical questions and mental health support, and that patients may benefit from options trading timeliness against human review.

Large language models are increasingly consulted for clinical decision support, yet the cost of the services or treatment they recommend had not been systematically compared with what treating physicians actually ordered. In NEJM AI, Dvir Aran, Jeremy D. Goldhaber-Fiebert, Ittai Many, Anthony Nguyen, Daniel Yang and Shahar Shelly report "Comparative Cost of Care Recommended by Large Language Models versus Treating Physicians."

The study pipeline runs in five steps: 200 cases were selected; each note was split into the clinical presentation and the assessment and plan; 24 AI systems generated plans under 3 prompts (standard, cost-aware and parsimonious-but-safe); orders were extracted (median of three extractions); and each order was priced from CPT codes against the Medicare fee schedule.

blocks.cap: Study workflow and an example case: a 2-month-old infant with classic bronchiolitis.

blocks.x: In the example case, the treating clinician ordered no diagnostic tests (US$0), since routine testing is not indicated for bronchiolitis. With the default prompt, the AI ordered a viral respiratory panel and an echocardiogram (US$454); the cost-aware prompt ordered a viral panel and pertussis PCR (US$292); the parsimonious prompt ordered a pertussis PCR test only (US$35).
